Jahnavi mol, come, sit with your Appachan. You asked why I always tell you to say what you see? I'll tell you. My name is Thomas, and when I was nine, in the little school by the paddy fields, our teacher drew three lines on the blackboard.
"Which is longest?" he asked. I could see it was the first one. Plain as day.
But the boy in front said, "The second." Then the next boy, and the next. Ten boys. All "the second."
My turn came. My ears were burning. I didn't want them to laugh at me.
"The second," I said.
The teacher measured with his ruler. The first one was longest. Everyone laughed at all of us, and I felt like a fool twice over.

qa.a: He drew three lines on the blackboard.

qa.q: Why did young Thomas say "the second" when he could see the first was longest?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at if he disagreed with ten boys, so he went along even though he saw the truth.

qa.q: What choice could young Thomas have made when his turn came?
qa.a: He could have said "the first" quietly and calmly, trusting his own eyes even if the others laughed.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the ten boys all saying the second line?

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a child following a group's wrong answer about which line is longest, afraid of being laughed at even though the truth was visible.

Tejas knew. They weighed the same. A kilo was a kilo. His father had shown him that once with the kitchen scale.

"Iron," he said.
"Wrong!" said the quiz master. "They weigh the same."
Tejas stared at the table. He had known.
